Q: Spring Securirty Granted Authorities always return empty A:

I don't know if you solved your problem. However, your description helped me to solve mine. I implemented the authorities mapper almost based on your code and it is working just fine. The only thing I can see that could lead to an empty authorities field is the field is empty when calling the mapper or none of the authorities in the argument map to your AD roles defined as ROLE_USER and ROLE_ADMIN.

Q: ORA-29548: Java system class reported: could not identify release specified in classes.bin A:

IF you have applied a recent PSU or java patch to your database make sure you have ran the @postinstall.sql. For example 20406220 has a postinstall.sql in Oracle_home/sqlpatch/20406220 directory.

Q: Independent y axes per facet colum with ggplot2::geom_density() and ggh4x::facet_grid2() A: 
... + 
ggh4x::facetted_pos_scales(y = list(
  name == "am" ~ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1)),
  name == "vs" ~ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1.5)) 
))

Edit - this is ugly as sin, but there's probably a much nicer way to do something equivalent. I build the original plots, extract the y ranges, calculate the max y per column, then make a list of scale_y_continuous specifications to add to the plot.

your_code -> a

a |> ggplot_build() -> b
b$layout$layout |> 
  cbind(sapply(1:12, \(x) b$layout$panel_scales_y[[x]]$range$range) |> t()) |>
  dplyr::mutate(max_y = max(`2`), .by = name) |>
  dplyr::pull(max_y) |>
  purrr::map(\(x) scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, x))) -> scales

a +
  ggh4x::facetted_pos_scales(y = scales)

Q: Is replaying a transactional outbox in auto-increment ID order sufficient to reproduce the source database state? A:

This can never work.

Imagine two concurrent transactions modifying two rows in the same table:

Transaction 1                         Transaction 2
=============                         =============

start transaction (event 101)
                                      start transaction (event 102)

update row 1

                                      update row 1

                                      update row 2

update row 2

write outbox
                                      write outbox
commit
                                      commit

Transaction 1 modifies row 1 before transaction 2 does, but transaction 2 modifies row 2 before transaction 1. No matter how you serialize these two transactions, the result would never be the same as the original.

The only way you could get this to work is to serialize the original transactions, so that no two of them can run concurrently. That is safe, but horrible for concurrency, particularly if these transactions are not very short.

One way to serialize transactions is to use advisory locks:

START TRANSACTION;

/*
 * Take a transaction-level advisory lock.
 * "4711" is an arbitrary number; you have to use the same
 * number in all transactions to use the same lock.
 */
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(4711);

/* get the event number */
SELECT nextval('event_sequence');

/* perform all your activities */
UPDATE ...;

INSERT INTO outbox VALUES (...);

COMMIT;

A potential alternative to strict serialization is to use the SERIALIZABLE isolation level for all your transactions. That will make sure that the transactions can be serialized (even if they run concurrently). But then you never know which transaction is logically earlier, so you don't know how to assign event numbers.
